title: How Date a Supermodel, Thanks To Academic Fraud in Medicine
subtitle: It's a cautionary tale...for the unambitious doctors who don't commit it.
body_html:
So I was listening to Freakonomics, like I do, just the other night. They have two phenomenal episodes about academic fraud. This podcast two-parter covers the story of Dan Ariely and Francesca Gino, two social scientists (one in good standing at Duke, and the other suspended from Harvard and suing them, in that order) regarding allegations of fraud in their research. Research regarding, among other things, academic fraud.

Gino even wrote a book about it! It’s called Rebel Talent: Why It Pays to Break the Rules at Work and In Life (that is an Amazon affiliate link for humor)… from her book promo material:

Gino argues that the future belongs to the rebel — and that there’s a rebel in each of us. We live in turbulent times, when competition is fierce, reputations are easily tarnished on social media, and the world is more divided than ever before. In this cutthroat environment, cultivating rebel talent is what allows businesses to evolve and to prosper. And rebellion has an added benefit beyond the workplace: it leads to a more vital, engaged, and fulfilling life.

Gino sued Harvard Business School for Defamation, a popular topic in this newsletter, and her suit was almost entirely dismissed. Recall. truth is an absolute defense in defamation cases. The judge ruled:

… Gino had failed to plausibly allege that the University defamed her, violated her privacy, or unlawfully interfered with her relationships with publishers.

Which, given the subtitle of her book alone, seems like an implausible case to win…and an even more weird case to litigate…Thus, this rebel without a cause of action… amended the remaining contract claim, rebel that she is, as a gender discrimination claim (from The Crimson):

Harvard breached its contract with her by subjecting her to disciplinary measures in violation of its own disciplinary and tenure policies.

Gino was accused of data fraud in 2021 by data investigation blog Data Colada, which said she falsified data across several academic studies. Harvard later conducted an internal investigation, placing Gino on administrative leave and initiating steps to revoke her tenure.

Are the cases of piracy-plagiarism-forgery that we know about only the tip of an iceberg? Why do such cases happen? Is the practice on the increase? And what role should the establishment, including the editors of medical journals and information retrieval systems, have in this? I could have written that series of sentences myself, but I plagiarized it1 to prove how easy it would be! It was easy but very dishonest, don’t you agree?

Share

Of course, this got me thinking about biomedical science. To quote with attribution:

Two cardinal rules of biomedical research are that scientists pursue absolute truthfulness and objectivity and that they report only honest data.

Yet in recent years, there has been evidence that these rules have been broken…

—Altman & Melcher, BMJ, 1983

The incentives are as pernicious as they are pervasive. Fame! H-index increases! It’s so absurdly easy, too; one Google search got me to a Co-authorship without any work.

We sell our prepared manuscripts for publication in the journals indexed in Scopus, Clarivate Analytics, Web of Science and other scientific databases. The manuscripts are already written and accepted by the journals. You can buy a whole manuscript or an author-place in the list of authors of the manuscript. You just need to pay, and we publish and index a manuscript with your name. Become a co-author of a prepared manuscript.

Oh, my.

I'm a prolific author, for readers who are just getting familiar with me—not just here, in this newsletter. Also, in academic publishing. Yes, I write this every day. In addition to that, published in 2024 alone, I cranked out the following:

Aslam, A., Shinozuka, K., Muir, O. S., & Tabaac, B. J. (2024). Mapping the Use of Ketamine in Treatment-Resistant Depression and Other Psychiatric Disorders: A Scoping Review of Practice Patterns, Efficacy, and Patient Demographic Trends.

LL Williams, C Fleisher, OS Muir, C Grimes, CM MacMillan, RA Dugger Basic Concepts in Mentalizing-Based Therapy for Emerging Personality Disorders AACAP's 2024 Annual Meeting

LL Williams, C Fleisher, E Bleiberg, OS Muir, C Grimes, RA Dugger Mentalizing-Based Therapy for Borderline Personality Disorder and Other “Difficult” Patients. AACAP's 2024 Annual Meeting

MacMillan, A., MacMillan, C., & Muir, O. (2024). ACCELERATED DTMS UTILIZATION OF H7 COIL FOR COMORBID TRD: A CASE SERIES. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, 1.

Aslam, A., Handoo, I., MacMillan, C., & Muir, O. (2024). SUCCESSFUL DTMS IN RTMS, ECT, AND KETAMINE REFRACTORY DEPRESSION: A CASE SERIES. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, 1.

Aslam, A. M., MacMillan, C., & Muir, O. (2024). UTILIZING NVNS TREATMENT EFFECTIVELY AFTER NON-RESPONSIVENESS TO ACCELERATED H7 AND H1 TREATMENT IN HIGHLY REFRACTORY MDD: A CASE REPORT. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, 1.

Tabaac, B. J., Shinozuka, K., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Psilocybin. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e121-e132.

Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—3, 4-Methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (MDMA). American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e141-e154.

Muir, O. S., Shinozuka, K., Beutler, B. D., Arenas, A., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Tabaac, B. J. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—The Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats of Psychedelic Therapeutics. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e178-e182.

Cherian, K., Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Ibogaine. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e133-e140.

Beutler, B. D., Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Arenas, A., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Lysergic Acid Diethylamide (LSD). American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e104-e111.

Evans, V. D., Arenas, A., Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Ketamine. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e155-e177.

Shinozuka, K., Tabaac, B. J., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—N, N-Dimethyltryptamine and Ayahuasca. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e112-e120.

Tabaac, B. J., Shinozuka, K., Arenas, A., Beutler, B. D., Cherian, K., Evans, V. D., ... & Muir, O. S. (2024). Psychedelic Therapy: A Primer for Primary Care Clinicians—Historical Perspective and Overview. American Journal of Therapeutics, 31(2), e97-e103.

DeSouza, D. D., Nakano, E., Hoang, V., Hoang, K., Ling, D., Muir, O., ... & Carreon, D. (2024). Real-World Outcomes and Predictors of Accelerated rTMS Treatment Response for Treatment-Resistant Depression. medRxiv, 2024-05.

And already in 2025, this has been published:

Tabaac, B. J., Feldman, M., & Muir, O. S. (2025). Informed Consent to Psychedelic Medicine. American Journal of Therapeutics, 32(1), e37-e39.

Readers might just be wondering how I got all that done.

THE OLD-FASHIONED WAY!

This is to say that I’m charismatic and good at wrangling much better writers and scientists than myself to coauthor papers with me. Do you see all those other names above? They are great scientists. I also do “crazy” things, like spending all of Thanksgiving 2023 editing away with my mom, Vita West Muir, an actual medical editor. But apparently, I missed a memo. Other people are making up the data or even buying their name on a paper someone else authored, soup to nuts.

That seems way easier. The incentives in academics are virtually all in favor of fraud, plagiarism, and nonsense on a massive scale. First, the business of academic publishing is a mind-blowingly profitable oligopoly:

The market is largely dominated by five large publishing houses: Elsevier, Black & Wiley, Taylor & Francis, Springer Nature and SAGE, which control more than 50 % of the market between them.

The largest is…

Elsevier has a profit margin approaching 40 %, which is higher than that of companies such as Microsoft, Google and Coca Cola, and the curve is pointing upward.

It has a market cap of $85b….yesterday:

The last time I wrote about the scam that is academic publishing, it was only $41/share. It’s like I’m some prophet for profits! What incentive do they have to publish fewer articles? None. Remember that those journals are edited overwhelmingly by clout chasers dumb enough to do it for free. They call their buddies to peer-review, also for free. Oh, wait, that includes me sometimes. Oh, my. This is a good scam. And with open-access journals, scientists pay thousands of dollars to get an article published in the first place! Without these publications, their career is dead, so it makes sense to take the chance to submit it. And with the volume of papers only growing, it is hard to detect fraud as a reviewer.

I know this because I also take the time to function as such a peer reviewer. We don’t usually get access to the raw data, and unsophisticates like myself would often barely know how to run the analysis on the raw data. I can read a meta-analysis and explain to my audience how to understand charts and graphs, as in my non-plagiarized book, Inessential Pharmacology. (amazon link). But I couldn't discern from a pile of raw data how to re-create it if I’m being very honest.

I don’t even use AI to write this newsletter. I'm banging on physical keys or dictating like a chump! Here is what I got for it over on Google Scholar:

And here is how Dr. Gino is doing, with her rule breakery:

Which is way…better. Here I am, “not-using-the-word-curing” depression with next-generation treatments, but a dud in academic medicine.

The incentives in academics are all in the direction of exciting findings—those get cited! Highly cited papers are excellent for the impact factor of journals. Everyone wants the outcome (clout) of continuing things just as they are. Highly cited scientists get tenure. Tenure means never having to say you are sorry. If that statement doesn’t land, please see Rebel Dr. Gino’s contract dispute above, in which firing her for being a fraud might not have followed the rules.

Academic medicine has created a system of incentives in which rule-observing people will do good work. Still, rule breakers will get ahead like a person with a dummy in the passenger seat gets to zoom past all the other losers on the highway in the HOV lane. It’s a setup for all of us to get scammed. This means we can’t know what to believe in medicine. I already had to issue one correction this past year regarding retracted papers on MDMA (my article is still working its way into the journal).

In biomedical science, these findings can be catastrophic—such as fraudulent papers citing a non-existent link between autism and vaccines:

In a statement published on Feb. 2, the British medical journal said that it is now clear that “several elements” of a 1998 paper it published by Dr. Andrew Wakefield and his colleagues (Lancet 1998;351[9103]:637–41) “are incorrect, contrary to the findings of an earlier investigation.”2

Andrew Wakefield’s now-retracted and fraudulent paper led to a cascade of negative public perception that was felt immediately— and to this day:

AW98 [Ed: the 1998 paper by Wakefield suggesting a link between MMR and Autism] led to an immediate increase of about 70 MMR injury claims cases per month, averaging across six estimation strategies (meta-analytic effect = 70.44 [52.19, 88.75], p < 0.01). Preliminary evidence suggests that the volume of negative media attention to MMR increased in the weeks following AW98’s publication across four estimation strategies (meta-analytic effect = 9.59% [3.66, 15.51], p < 0.01).3

Fake papers create more adverse reporting in the real world. Although it will be hard for Andrew Wakefield to get another academic gig, most academic fraud will never be discovered—the most likely outcome for fraudsters is a long and successful career.

All the incentives are aligned to reward splashy findings, impressive results, and more well-cited publications. And Wakefield?

His punishment for Academic Fraud is dating Elle Macpherson—yes, the supermodel—and he gets to be a star or anti-hero, depending on your worldview. And he might even be responsible for her eventual death:

In fact, when diagnosed [with breast cancer] in 2018, [Macpherson] was in a relationship with Wakefield, a strong advocate of this ideology

Regardless, he’s more of a star than most academics. The rewards just aren’t as robust for boringness and honesty, while they are replete for flashy fraud. We all suffer on account of it. This is why replication of studies by independent investigators matters, and perhaps the media can cover debunkers, replicators, and fact-checkers with the breathless enthusiasm we typically reserve for new and exciting findings.

A physician-scientist can only hope.

1

Altman L, Melcher L. Fraud in science. Br Med J (Clin Res Ed). 1983 Jun 25;286(6383):2003-6. doi: 10.1136/bmj.286.6383.2003. PMID: 6409204; PMCID: PMC1548517.

2

Eggertson L. Lancet retracts 12-year-old article linking autism to MMR vaccines. CMAJ. 2010 Mar 9;182(4):E199-200. doi: 10.1503/cmaj.109-3179. Epub 2010 Feb 8. PMID: 20142376; PMCID: PMC2831678.

3
